What does the bar above word docs do? There are 2 adjusters, a bar and an arrow, what do they do?
They set the margins, like the mechanical thing on old mechanical typewriters.

^^This.

You can slide the ruler guides or double click on the ruler itself to enter your margin preferences.
Margins for what? There are many margins for different formatting within documents. Which bars/arrows do what?

These are throwbacks to the days of typewriters and are used to control indents and tabs. The top bar sets the left indent of the first line of a paragraph. The bottom arrow sets the left indent of lines after the first line of a paragraph when the text wraps around at the right margin. You can also use the ruler bar to set multiple tab stops to vertically align things like tabular lists or tables without using an actual table in Word. There are several tab stop types including left, middle, right, decimal aligned and bar stops which allow for different kinds of tabular alignment.

Here is a sample of first and second line indents as well as left, middle, decimal, right and bar tab stops so you can see what the marks look like on the ruler bar and the results in a document. The idea came from this camping coffee thread and has been percolating through my brain since then. I think a cloth steeping bag would make for a very light and minimalist backpacking/camping coffee setup: no glass or specialized brewing apparatus to carry, your cooking pot does the work.

I sewed some teabags at the same time, because why not? The tea bags are a simple folded rectangle sewed up each side, no hem on the open top. They are a little small for anything but 1 or 2 cups of tea. Pic, with teaspoon and tea for scale.

The coffee bag is a narrow but deep round bottomed bag with a drawstring top. Pic, with coffee beans for atmosphere.

I was hoping to make the coffee bag wider than it turned out. My base piece was 11cm across but the side piece wasn't long enough for that, minus hem allowances, and minus even more for the wandering stitch as I struggled to line up the base and side pieces (I hadn't enough pins). It ended up much narrower. I think a tapered bag (wider at the mouth) would work even better for getting grounds in and out of the bag. Having the ability to invert the bag mouth over the lip of the brew pot would be nice to avoid having to hold the bag you're pouring hot water into. At any rate, wider than 9-10cm would be nice and it doesn't have to be as deep as this one turned out (20cm).

The coffee it makes is more like drip coffee with sediment than french press which is a little unexpected since the brewing method is all french press but for the bagged grounds.
